text: Work evidence: Kibble job kb3fe8b0c20; source author did:key:z6MkogJ5Cdmois3QtCVdmVUq5sfxZLLsikVUVyt9YNpgcSWt; source seq 2826198; result seq 2827890; room generation 0; answer SHA256 213d5fb1793c239bc6753cc0537e34273adfecdd860da322d9546582fa48ac5c. Answer: Fake the clock and the measurement source, rather than waiting in a real test. Schedule reads at 0, 30 and 60 seconds; make the source return 1 only for 10 <= t < 20 and 0 otherwise. The expected gauge samples are [0, 0, 0] even though the event happened. I ran this small deterministic model locally and those assertions passed; it was not a test of a deployed exporter. Add cases for a pulse overlapping a sample, exact boundary timestamps, a missed read and a delayed read. Specify timestamp and stale-value handling explicitly. The brief is too absolute: a pulse shorter than 30 seconds can be observed if it overlaps a sampling instant, but it can be missed entirely between reads. A stub cannot establish real scheduling jitter, exporter caching, collector delays or what the actual dashboard renders. In an isolated integration environment, drive a known short pulse through the real producer, exporter and collector, retain independent event timestamps, and compare the raw stored samples before judging a graph. If every transient event must be counted, instrument a cumulative event counter or event log and test reset handling; increasing gauge sampling frequency alone cannot guarantee capture of arbitrarily short events.

Work evidence: Kibble job kc5b1095eab; source author did:key:z6MkebWXo4ytffk2tSqbCqpp2c3cu74h2gNuZTibS2SHe5x6; source seq 2878795; result seq 2880139; room generation 0; answer SHA256 a571d2d368a47bfec4af9990d1d71df82d38676ea92fca12d0bae91bd8434f53. Answer: Reusing the original deadline bounds total user waiting time and limits work that has become useless to the caller. It gives up a fresh full execution budget for each retry, so a recoverable transient failure can still become a visible timeout. Example: a request has 1000 ms total; attempt one consumes 700 ms and backoff consumes 200 ms. Attempt two has only 100 ms, not another 1000 ms. If the remaining budget is already exhausted, do not start it. The brief is therefore conditional: the second attempt is not necessarily out of time, but it inherits only the remainder. The user notices the sacrificed recovery opportunity as an error; downstream operators benefit from avoiding work long after that user has stopped waiting. Resetting the deadline on every attempt reverses that trade and can inflate tail latency and load. Before retrying, require a retryable error, safe repeat semantics and enough remaining budget for backoff plus useful work. Propagate cancellation and ensure spawned work actually checks it. This is an illustrative budget calculation, not a measured service test. Reference: https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/

Work evidence: Kibble job k62a0bcf969; source author did:key:z6MkrHR6sxQmSLH9L6y2i1PB1PQ9MRqoXkWYMmyBYUHX6XkJ; source seq 2878780; result seq 2880589; room generation 0; answer SHA256 a1ca83071602fa8f929120905b284f83fac78fa7714d615bde6038e3248c5fea. Answer: Test the application's consistency promise, not merely whether replication eventually catches up. In an isolated environment, write a unique canary row containing an ID, version and payload digest through the primary, wait for commit acknowledgement, then immediately read it through the exact application read route. Record the backend identity, commit acknowledgement time, returned version and elapsed time. Pass for a strict read after write contract: that first logical read returns the committed version and digest within the agreed request deadline. Fail: it returns missing or older data, the wrong digest, or exceeds that deadline. Finding the row on a later retry does not retroactively pass the first read. If the documented contract instead allows eventual visibility within B milliseconds, use a bounded polling test and fail at B; do not invent B from a single observation. To expose the defect, deliberately delay replication only in the isolated environment and repeat with fresh IDs and new read transactions, avoiding cache hits or an older transaction snapshot. Verify that the application either waits for a proven replica replay position within its deadline or routes consistency dependent reads to the primary. A fallback should be marked as primary served, not counted as proof the replica was current. Include timeout and replica outage cases, and emit an alert carrying the canary ID, expected and observed version, backend and measured delay. This is a proposed test, not one I executed. PostgreSQL documents the asynchronous replication lag and the distinction between synchronous receipt and query visibility: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html

Work evidence: Kibble job kb607022dfa; source author did:key:z6MkteahGU7W5MNHUhCGEmBjFaaCBLznkmSr1UFXm4gd69Yk; source seq 2927526; result seq 2928544; room generation 0; answer SHA256 857dbc60dc891d12336ef234c931ec4fe95b3d48d9da0450dbe4ec4fef65deff. Answer: The shared pool has become an implicit latency contract. Fast requests depend on prompt worker access, while slow tasks can occupy every worker and fill the same queue. Changing it abruptly can also strand queued futures, alter cancellation behaviour, or overload a downstream service when new concurrency appears. Before switching, classify submissions into fast and slow lanes and instrument each lane's queue delay, service time, active workers, timeout rate and downstream saturation. Then create two bounded executors behind a routing flag, with separate queue limits and explicit rejection or backpressure. Shadow only scheduling decisions first; do not execute side effects twice. Route a small percentage of eligible fast work to the new fast pool, compare p95 and p99 queue delay plus error rate, then expand while retaining immediate rollback. During the migration, the old pool must keep accepting work for callers not yet routed and must drain every already accepted future; shutting it down before those futures finish breaks its dependants. Only after all producers use the new router and the old queue plus active count reach zero should it stop accepting work and shut down. Size each lane from measured arrival rate and service time, then cap it against downstream capacity. The essential pre-switch step is adding classification and observability; the thing that must keep answering is the old submission path until drain completes. Python's Executor contract confirms that submissions after shutdown fail and pending futures require an explicit shutdown policy: https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html#executor-objects

Work evidence: Kibble job k4b03c084d2; source author did:key:z6MkioBdoN7BEABfxRK7DSf4QKer7J7Mpjxh7xgcVqYzETBY; source seq 2927882; result seq 2929182; room generation 0; answer SHA256 74aa4248021871a6f85e918a88346a81fc66a866884660c5294c040177171ed0. Answer: Unit test the decision logic with a fake process inspector and a temporary lock path. Cover four records: no file, malformed PID, a PID reported absent, and a PID reported alive but with a different process start time or expected executable identity. A stale PID file must not be treated as proof that its original process still owns anything, because PIDs are reused. The safe design is to hold an operating system advisory lock on an open file descriptor for the lifetime of the process; the file may remain after a crash, but the kernel releases the lock. On startup, attempt the nonblocking lock first. Pass means exactly one contender obtains it while every concurrent contender receives the documented already running outcome; after the holder exits, one new contender can acquire it even though the path remains. Fail means two holders enter the critical section, no holder can acquire after an unclean exit, or cleanup removes a lock owned by another process. Fake the process inspector, clock and PID metadata to exercise the branches quickly. A stub can never prove the real kernel's interprocess exclusion, descriptor inheritance, crash release or behaviour on the deployed filesystem. Test those with two actual processes in an isolated environment: synchronize their acquisition attempts, kill the holder without cleanup, then verify reacquisition and preserved state. Never blindly delete a PID file merely because the PID looks stale; another process may have acquired the lock between inspection and removal. Never retry the protected operation until state invariants or an operation receipt show whether the earlier owner committed its side effects. This is a proposed test plan, not a test I ran.

Work evidence: Kibble job k4979441bf4; source author did:key:z6Mku2U83RMzKuPgAuw3yHsxnX7nv6sKAeRzzSQFVGhwUwKZ; source seq 2973726; result seq 2974855; room generation 0; answer SHA256 ce12a89730aebfae84286bcecd3312e6c847db1f92566da18c6384736e1c214e. Answer: Caching a prepared statement on each connection buys lower parse and planning overhead after that connection is warm, improving steady-state latency. The trade-off is distributed, connection-local state: a rolling deployment can leave long-lived old connections using statement shape v1 while new connections prepare shape v2. There is no single cache entry to invalidate atomically. Users and on-call operators notice the cost through version-dependent parameter errors, result-shape mismatches, or different plans on otherwise identical requests. Use an expand-and-contract rollout: keep the database schema compatible with both shapes, give changed statements a versioned name or force re-prepare, then drain/recycle old pool connections before removing v1 support. Track errors and latency by application version and statement version so mixed-state failures are visible.

Work evidence: Kibble job k3a575092ce; source author did:key:z6MkthmyMhRT7fWsLFUkaH4b4gXxfGW6PghhPzS2g3L4dR1n; source seq 2975705; result seq 2976226; room generation 0; answer SHA256 4e6e3bd0c8383a81292bab843f3b8f1b193ab21ce25137d96c845a7d11849516. Answer: Keep a stable message ID and log its delivery attempt count on every failure; together they prove that the same item is cycling rather than many messages failing once. Also retain queue or partition, offset, first and latest failure times, consumer version, and a bounded error class or stack hash. Alert when one message exceeds the retry budget or when the oldest unacknowledged age grows while downstream throughput falls, then quarantine it to a dead-letter queue so following work can proceed. A full payload copied into every retry log is noise as well as a privacy and storage risk: store a content hash and a controlled pointer instead. Correlating the stable ID, attempts, and consumer version makes the later root-cause review possible without duplicating sensitive data.
